sections.heading: Living on small mercies while I wait for fullness
sections.text:
Lord, life here feels so limited. I am like a fish kept alive in a small bowl of water, while you are preparing an ocean for me. I have enough breath to keep going, but one day I will breathe the clean, free air of your presence. Here you give me a shaft of light in my darkness and enough warmth to keep my heart from freezing. There, with you, I will live in light and warmth forever.

Thank you for every mercy that keeps me alive now. But do not let me mistake these small mercies for the fullness you have promised.
theological_themes: Earthly life gives real but limited foretastes of the fullness of life with God.
Heaven is not merely relief from hardship but the full enjoyment of God's presence.
Present grace sustains believers while they wait for complete redemption.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts life in the present body with the believer's future dwelling from God and speaks of longing to be at home with the Lord. This supports the prayer's sense of present limitation and future fullness in God's presence.

John describes the new creation as filled with God's own glory and light, needing no lesser source of illumination. This grounds the prayer's movement from a small beam of light now to everlasting light with God.

sections.heading: Asking you to change what I want
sections.text:
Father, my natural wants are not safe guides. So many of them are twisted, impatient, selfish, and aimed at the wrong things. It is mercy when you put those desires to death, even when it feels painful.

But the longings in me that reach toward you are gifts from your hand. You planted them; please keep watering them. Wake up in me a stronger hunger and thirst for your kingdom. Make me want what is above more than what only keeps me occupied here.
theological_themes: Sin disorders human desire, and God mercifully puts sinful desires to death.
Holy desires for God are created and sustained by God's grace.
The believer asks for deeper longing for the kingdom of God and things above.

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers, because they have been raised with Christ, to seek the things above and to put earthly sinful desires to death. This closely matches the prayer's request for corrupt desires to be destroyed and heavenly desires to grow.
Paul describes the conflict between the desires of the flesh and the desires of the Spirit. This supports the prayer's distinction between disordered natural desires and God-given spiritual longings.

sections.heading: Choosing you over the world
sections.text:
Here I can have pieces of the world. There I will have you, fully and forever, in Christ. Here my life is full of wanting, waiting, asking, and praying. There I will be completely secure, with no suspicion that you might turn me away, and no prayer that conflicts with your good will.

The comforts I have now are often mixed things. They can help me, but they can also weigh me down. With you there will be joy without sorrow, comfort without pain, love that never cools, and rest that never wears out.
theological_themes: Christ is the believer's true and final portion, greater than the world and its comforts.
Present comforts are mixed with weakness, sorrow, and burden, but future life with God will be unmixed joy and rest.
Prayer now is marked by longing and dependence; in glory the believer will enjoy complete security and fellowship with God.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist confesses that God himself is his supreme desire and portion, even above everything on earth. This supports the prayer's contrast between having the world now and having God in Christ forever.

Paul says believers groan inwardly as they wait for the full redemption still to come. This fits the prayer's description of earthly life as longing, waiting, and prayer before the fullness of heaven.
The promised dwelling of God with his people includes the removal of death, mourning, crying, and pain. This directly supports the prayer's hope for joy without sorrow and comfort without suffering.

sections.heading: Let me know what is waiting with you
sections.text:
Lord, help me know—not just as an idea, but deep in my heart—that heaven is all love. There I will see your beauty without a veil, and seeing you will fill my whole soul with delight.

Help me know that heaven is all peace. No error, pride, rebellion, anger, or restless passion will rise up there.

Help me know that heaven is all joy. Faith will have reached its goal. Fasting, praying, mourning, humbling myself, staying watchful, fearing, and complaining will all be finished. Bring me safely there, in your time, and keep my heart turned toward that home until I arrive.
theological_themes: Heaven is the unhindered vision and enjoyment of God's beauty.
In glory, sin and its inner turmoil will be gone completely.
The disciplines and sorrows of the present life will give way to the completed joy of communion with God.
Longing for heaven is held together with trust in God's timing.

scripture_references.connection: John teaches that believers will be like Christ when they see him as he is, and that this hope purifies them now. This grounds the prayer's desire to behold God's beauty and be transformed by that hope.
Peter speaks of believers loving Christ now without seeing him and receiving the outcome of faith. This connects with the prayer's claim that heaven is the end or goal of believing.
Jude praises God as the one able to keep his people and present them blameless with great joy. This supports the prayer's final request to be brought safely into God's presence.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original line asking God to 'lead me to it soon' could be misread as a desire for death apart from trust in God's providential timing. I preserved the longing for heaven while making explicit submission to God's timing.

The statement that natural desires are corrupt and that it is God's mercy to destroy them can sound like created bodily desires are evil in themselves. I rendered this as disordered sinful desires, which preserves the Puritan emphasis on indwelling sin without implying that creation or embodiment is inherently bad.

The phrase 'asking without refusal' needed nuance so it would not suggest heaven as a place where God grants any autonomous wish. I framed it as prayer perfectly aligned with God's good will and complete security in his welcome.
significant_interpretive_choices: I kept the concrete images of the fish in a small vessel, limited air, and a beam of sun, but expressed them in ordinary contemporary speech rather than as a line-by-line paraphrase.
I interpreted 'the eye affects the heart' as the transforming joy of seeing God's beauty, connected to the traditional Christian hope of seeing God and being changed.

I treated the list of present practices—believing, fasting, praying, mourning, humbling, watching, fearing, repining—as the burdens and disciplines of life before glory, not as things despised, but as things fulfilled and surpassed in God's presence.
